questions.question: Define a hydrocarbon.
questions.modelAnswer: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
markingPoints: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

questions.question: Why is crude oil described as a finite resource?
questions.modelAnswer: It forms over millions of years and is used much faster than it is naturally replaced.
markingPoints: It forms over millions of years and is used much faster than it is naturally replaced.

questions.question: Give the molecular formula of hexane.
questions.modelAnswer:
Alkanes have formula CnH2n+2.
For n=6 the formula is C6H14.
markingPoints: Alkanes have formula CnH2n+2.
For n=6 the formula is C6H14.

questions.question: What is a homologous series?
questions.modelAnswer: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties.
markingPoints: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties.

questions.question: Explain why incomplete combustion of fuels can be dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer: It can produce carbon monoxide, which is toxic because it reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. It can also produce particulates that damage the lungs.
markingPoints: It can produce carbon monoxide, which is toxic because it reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. It can also produce particulates that damage the lungs.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of propane.
questions.modelAnswer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
markingPoints: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.

questions.question: Explain why crude oil is described as both a fuel resource and a feedstock, and evaluate one reason for conserving it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fractions burn to release energy.
Molecules are starting materials for polymers/solvents/detergents.
Finite, environmental impacts/CO2, and higher-value chemical uses support conservation.
markingPoints: Fractions burn to release energy.
Molecules are starting materials for polymers/solvents/detergents.
Finite, environmental impacts/CO2, and higher-value chemical uses support conservation.

questions.question: Compare complete and incomplete combustion in terms of oxygen supply, products, energy release and environmental effects.
questions.modelAnswer:
Plentiful O2 gives CO2+H2O and more complete energy transfer.
Limited O2 gives CO and/or carbon+H2O and less energy.
CO toxic, soot respiratory/global dimming, CO2 greenhouse gas.
markingPoints: Plentiful O2 gives CO2+H2O and more complete energy transfer.
Limited O2 gives CO and/or carbon+H2O and less energy.
CO toxic, soot respiratory/global dimming, CO2 greenhouse gas.

questions.question: Draw in words/describe the displayed formulae and general formulae of the first four alkanes and alkenes, and explain saturated versus unsaturated.
questions.modelAnswer:
Alkanes CH4,C2H6,C3H8,C4H10.
CnH2n+2, only C-C single bonds/saturated.
Alkenes C2H4,C3H6,C4H8,C5H10.
CnH2n, contain C=C/unsaturated.
markingPoints: Alkanes CH4,C2H6,C3H8,C4H10.
CnH2n+2, only C-C single bonds/saturated.
Alkenes C2H4,C3H6,C4H8,C5H10.
CnH2n, contain C=C/unsaturated.

questions.question: Describe how crude oil can be separated by fractional distillation and identify the measurement on which separation depends.
questions.modelAnswer:
Heat crude oil so most vaporises.
Vapours enter a column hot at the bottom and cooler at the top.
Fractions condense at different heights and are drawn off.
Separation depends on different boiling-point ranges.
markingPoints: Heat crude oil so most vaporises.
Vapours enter a column hot at the bottom and cooler at the top.
Fractions condense at different heights and are drawn off.
Separation depends on different boiling-point ranges.

questions.question: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Crude oil is vaporised and enters a column hot at bottom/cooler at top.
Hydrocarbons have different boiling points.
Vapours rise and condense where temperature falls below their boiling point.
Fractions are collected at different heights.
markingPoints: Crude oil is vaporised and enters a column hot at bottom/cooler at top.
Hydrocarbons have different boiling points.
Vapours rise and condense where temperature falls below their boiling point.
Fractions are collected at different heights.

questions.question: Explain why a fraction from crude oil contains several hydrocarbons rather than one compound.
questions.modelAnswer: A fraction contains hydrocarbons with similar boiling points. It condenses over a range of temperatures, not at one precise temperature.
markingPoints: A fraction contains hydrocarbons with similar boiling points. It condenses over a range of temperatures, not at one precise temperature.

questions.question: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil.
questions.modelAnswer: Crude oil is heated so most of it vaporises. Vapours rise through a fractionating column and cool. Different hydrocarbons condense at different heights because they have different boiling points.
markingPoints: Crude oil is heated so most of it vaporises. Vapours rise through a fractionating column and cool. Different hydrocarbons condense at different heights because they have different boiling points.

questions.question: Why do long-chain hydrocarbons have higher boiling points than short-chain hydrocarbons?
questions.modelAnswer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is required to overcome these forces.
markingPoints: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is required to overcome these forces.

questions.question: Write the balanced equation for complete combustion of propane and explain why incomplete combustion is dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer:
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
Limited oxygen can form carbon monoxide, which binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport.
Soot particulates can damage lungs.
markingPoints: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
Limited oxygen can form carbon monoxide, which binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport.
Soot particulates can damage lungs.

questions.question: State how alkane boiling point changes as chain length increases.
questions.modelAnswer: It increases.
markingPoints: It increases.

questions.question: State how alkane viscosity changes as chain length increases.
questions.modelAnswer: It increases.
markingPoints: It increases.

questions.question: State how alkane volatility changes as chain length increases.
questions.modelAnswer: It decreases.
markingPoints: It decreases.

questions.question: Explain why these trends occur.
questions.modelAnswer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.
markingPoints: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.question: Plan a fair comparison of the viscosity of several hydrocarbon liquids using a falling-sphere method.
questions.modelAnswer:
Use equal liquid depths in identical tubes at the same temperature.
Release the same sphere from the same point.
Time travel between fixed marks.
Repeat and calculate means.
Control temperature because viscosity changes with it.
markingPoints: Use equal liquid depths in identical tubes at the same temperature.
Release the same sphere from the same point.
Time travel between fixed marks.
Repeat and calculate means.
Control temperature because viscosity changes with it.

questions.question: Describe the test for an alkene and state the positive result.
questions.modelAnswer: Shake with bromine water. An alkene changes orange bromine water to colourless.
markingPoints: Shake with bromine water. An alkene changes orange bromine water to colourless.

questions.question: State the conditions used for catalytic cracking.
questions.modelAnswer: Vaporise the hydrocarbon and pass the vapour over a hot catalyst such as silica or alumina.
markingPoints: Vaporise the hydrocarbon and pass the vapour over a hot catalyst such as silica or alumina.

questions.question: Define cracking and state the products formed when a long-chain hydrocarbon is cracked.
questions.modelAnswer: Cracking is the breaking of long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter molecules. It produces shorter alkanes and alkenes.
markingPoints: Cracking is the breaking of long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter molecules. It produces shorter alkanes and alkenes.

questions.question: Explain why cracking produces useful products and state suitable conditions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Long-chain hydrocarbons are less useful.
Cracking forms shorter alkanes used as fuels and alkenes used for polymers.
Vaporised hydrocarbons pass over a hot catalyst, or are mixed with steam at high temperature.
markingPoints: Long-chain hydrocarbons are less useful.
Cracking forms shorter alkanes used as fuels and alkenes used for polymers.
Vaporised hydrocarbons pass over a hot catalyst, or are mixed with steam at high temperature.

questions.question: Decane cracks to form ethene and one other hydrocarbon. Deduce the formula of the other hydrocarbon.
questions.modelAnswer: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₂H₄ + C₈H₁₈, so the other hydrocarbon is C₈H₁₈.
markingPoints: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₂H₄ + C₈H₁₈, so the other hydrocarbon is C₈H₁₈.

questions.question: Describe how bromine water distinguishes ethene from the alkane made when decane cracks.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethene decolourises orange bromine water. The alkane does not change the colour under these conditions.
markingPoints: Ethene decolourises orange bromine water. The alkane does not change the colour under these conditions.

questions.question:
A refinery has excess long-chain fractions but high demand for petrol and alkene feedstock.
Explain cracking, give suitable conditions and identify the useful product types.
questions.modelAnswer:
Vaporise long-chain hydrocarbons.
High temperature over catalyst or steam cracking.
C-C bonds break.
Shorter alkanes are fuels and alkenes make polymers/chemicals.
markingPoints: Vaporise long-chain hydrocarbons.
High temperature over catalyst or steam cracking.
C-C bonds break.
Shorter alkanes are fuels and alkenes make polymers/chemicals.

questions.question: Describe how to test experimentally whether cracking products contain alkenes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pass vapour from heated hydrocarbon over a hot catalyst.
Collect gaseous products safely.
Shake a sample with bromine water.
Decolourisation from orange to colourless indicates a carbon–carbon double bond.
markingPoints: Pass vapour from heated hydrocarbon over a hot catalyst.
Collect gaseous products safely.
Shake a sample with bromine water.
Decolourisation from orange to colourless indicates a carbon–carbon double bond.

questions.question: Explain why bromine-water decolourisation alone does not identify which alkene is present.
questions.modelAnswer:
Many alkenes contain a C=C bond and give the same positive result.
The test identifies unsaturation, not a unique molecular identity.
Further analytical evidence is needed.
markingPoints: Many alkenes contain a C=C bond and give the same positive result.
The test identifies unsaturation, not a unique molecular identity.
Further analytical evidence is needed.

questions.question: Describe the bromine-water test for an alkene.
questions.modelAnswer:
Shake with orange bromine water.
An alkene decolourises it to colourless.
markingPoints: Shake with orange bromine water.
An alkene decolourises it to colourless.

questions.question:
A molecular formula is C5H10.
Explain why the formula alone does not prove the substance is an alkene and give evidence that would support identification.
questions.modelAnswer:
Matches CnH2n but could be cyclic/isomer.
Formula alone insufficient.
Displayed structure showing C=C, bromine-water decolourisation, or suitable spectroscopy/chemical evidence supports.
markingPoints: Matches CnH2n but could be cyclic/isomer.
Formula alone insufficient.
Displayed structure showing C=C, bromine-water decolourisation, or suitable spectroscopy/chemical evidence supports.

questions.question: Name the product formed when ethene reacts with steam.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol.
markingPoints: Ethanol.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the hydration of ethene.
questions.modelAnswer: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH.
markingPoints: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH.

questions.question: Ethene reacts with bromine. Name the product and state the type of reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: 1,2-dibromoethane is formed. This is an addition reaction.
markingPoints: 1,2-dibromoethane is formed. This is an addition reaction.

questions.question: Ethene reacts with hydrogen. Name the product and state the type of reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethane is formed. This is an addition reaction.
markingPoints: Ethane is formed. This is an addition reaction.

questions.question: Ethene reacts with steam. Name the product and state the type of reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol is formed. This is an addition reaction.
markingPoints: Ethanol is formed. This is an addition reaction.

questions.question: State the functional group in an alcohol.
questions.modelAnswer: The hydroxyl group, –OH.
markingPoints: The hydroxyl group, –OH.

questions.question: Compare ethanol manufacture by fermentation and hydration of ethene, including raw materials, conditions, rate, purity, energy, continuity and sustainability.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fermentation: renewable sugar, yeast, anaerobic 30-40 C, slow/batch, dilute ethanol needs distillation.
Hydration: ethene+steam, high T/P, catalyst, fast/continuous, purer product, finite crude-oil feedstock, higher energy.
Balanced judgement.
markingPoints: Fermentation: renewable sugar, yeast, anaerobic 30-40 C, slow/batch, dilute ethanol needs distillation.
Hydration: ethene+steam, high T/P, catalyst, fast/continuous, purer product, finite crude-oil feedstock, higher energy.
Balanced judgement.

questions.question: Describe the oxidation of ethanol.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ethanol reacts with an oxidising agent/oxygen to form ethanoic acid.
Complete combustion instead forms carbon dioxide and water.
markingPoints: Ethanol reacts with an oxidising agent/oxygen to form ethanoic acid.
Complete combustion instead forms carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: Explain why a distillation temperature that rises during collection suggests the sample is a mixture rather than a pure liquid.
questions.modelAnswer:
A pure liquid boils at a sharp, constant temperature at fixed pressure.
A mixture contains components with different boiling points, so vapour composition and temperature change during distillation.
markingPoints: A pure liquid boils at a sharp, constant temperature at fixed pressure.
A mixture contains components with different boiling points, so vapour composition and temperature change during distillation.

questions.question: Compare fermentation and hydration for manufacturing ethanol.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fermentation uses renewable sugar, low temperature/pressure but is slow, batch, makes dilute impure ethanol and needs distillation.
Hydration uses ethene from crude oil, high temperature/pressure and catalyst but is fast, continuous and makes purer ethanol.
Choice depends on feedstock, energy and scale.
markingPoints: Fermentation uses renewable sugar, low temperature/pressure but is slow, batch, makes dilute impure ethanol and needs distillation.
Hydration uses ethene from crude oil, high temperature/pressure and catalyst but is fast, continuous and makes purer ethanol.
Choice depends on feedstock, energy and scale.

questions.question: Compare how yield, rate, purity and energy use should be considered when evaluating fermentation and hydration routes to ethanol.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fermentation uses renewable sugars and lower temperature but is slow, produces dilute ethanol and needs purification.
Hydration is fast and continuous and produces purer ethanol but uses high temperature/pressure and non-renewable ethene.
A conclusion depends on weighted criteria and data.
markingPoints: Fermentation uses renewable sugars and lower temperature but is slow, produces dilute ethanol and needs purification.
Hydration is fast and continuous and produces purer ethanol but uses high temperature/pressure and non-renewable ethene.
A conclusion depends on weighted criteria and data.

questions.question: State the functional group in a carboxylic acid.
questions.modelAnswer: The carboxyl group, –COOH.
markingPoints: The carboxyl group, –COOH.

questions.question: Name the ester formed from ethanol and ethanoic acid.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethyl ethanoate (and water is also formed).
markingPoints: Ethyl ethanoate (and water is also formed).

questions.question: Explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids.
questions.modelAnswer: They only partially ionise in water, so only some molecules release hydrogen ions.
markingPoints: They only partially ionise in water, so only some molecules release hydrogen ions.

questions.question: Predict the products when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol.
questions.modelAnswer: An ester and water are formed.
markingPoints: An ester and water are formed.

questions.question: Predict the products when a carboxylic acid reacts with sodium carbonate.
questions.modelAnswer: A salt, water and carbon dioxide are formed.
markingPoints: A salt, water and carbon dioxide are formed.

questions.question: Identify the monomer used to make poly(ethene).
questions.modelAnswer: Ethene.
markingPoints: Ethene.

questions.question: Explain why most addition polymers are unreactive.
questions.modelAnswer: Their carbon backbone contains strong carbon–carbon single bonds and they have no reactive double-bond functional group.
markingPoints: Their carbon backbone contains strong carbon–carbon single bonds and they have no reactive double-bond functional group.

questions.question: Describe how propene forms poly(propene), including what changes at the double bond and how a correct repeating unit is shown.
questions.modelAnswer:
Many propene monomers.
C=C opens to C-C
No atoms lost.
Repeating unit [-CH2-CH(CH3)-]n with brackets, continuation bonds and n.
markingPoints: Many propene monomers.
C=C opens to C-C
No atoms lost.
Repeating unit [-CH2-CH(CH3)-]n with brackets, continuation bonds and n.

questions.question: Compare addition and condensation polymerisation, including monomers, products and whether a small molecule forms.
questions.modelAnswer:
Addition: unsaturated alkene monomers, one polymer product, no small molecule.
Condensation: monomers with two functional groups, polymer plus small molecule such as water.
May use two monomer types.
markingPoints: Addition: unsaturated alkene monomers, one polymer product, no small molecule.
Condensation: monomers with two functional groups, polymer plus small molecule such as water.
May use two monomer types.

questions.question: Describe how a diol and dicarboxylic acid form a polyester.
questions.modelAnswer: Their functional groups react repeatedly to form ester links and water.
markingPoints: Their functional groups react repeatedly to form ester links and water.

questions.question: Describe how amino acids form a polypeptide.
questions.modelAnswer: Amino and carboxyl groups react repeatedly to form peptide links and water.
markingPoints: Amino and carboxyl groups react repeatedly to form peptide links and water.

questions.question: Deduce the monomer used to make poly(propene) and describe the structural change during polymerisation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Monomer is propene, CH₂=CHCH₃.
The C=C double bond opens.
Many monomers join into a saturated chain with repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
markingPoints: Monomer is propene, CH₂=CHCH₃.
The C=C double bond opens.
Many monomers join into a saturated chain with repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
